glossario.la Madre: 母さま (kaa-sama: the honorific -sama of a local deity, like the names of Japanese folk-horror beings)
glossario.il telone: シート (always with «hide under / burrow under», so it never reads as «seat»)
glossario.la luce / la lampara: ライト (luce al massimo: ライト全開)
glossario.ferrare: 合わせる (the anglers' word; the first «Ha abboccato!» hint teaches it: 食いついた！ クリックかスペースで合わせる)
glossario.la barca / la prua / la poppa / il bordo: 船 / 船首 / 船尾 / 船べり
glossario.Notte N (HUD, intro, Catalogo): ナイト N (like ステージ N in Japanese games)
glossario.Tutti a 0/5/10/20: オール0/5/10/20 (what Japanese FNAF players call the 20/20/20/20 custom night)
glossario.Chi c'è c'è, chi non c'è non c'è!: もういいかい？ (what the seeker calls in Japanese hide-and-seek)
glossario.la conta di Hatch (Uno… Dieci!): いーち… にーい… … じゅう！ (the hide-and-seek way of counting)
glossario.Gazzetta del Golfo: 湾岸新報 (translated like the English «Gulf Gazette»)
glossario.le famiglie: 骸骨 / ゾンビ / グリッチ / 異形 / 流血
glossario.le rarità: ふつう / ややレア / レア / 伝説
glossario.tu (il giocatore): きみ, only where the sentence needs it (Japanese usually leaves «you» out); the radio voice gives plain curt orders (〜しろ / 〜するな), the hints use 〜して / 〜しないで
glossario.nomi propri: kept in Latin letters, with a half-width space before and after inside Japanese text (Gulpy は…, Splashland の…): easier to read, and the synthetic radio voice skips Latin letters glued to Japanese characters

note: Points a native speaker should check. (1) 母さま for «la Madre»: alternatives were マザー (too sci-fi) and おかあさま (too childish for the radio voice). (2) Night labels: HUD/intro 「ナイト 1」 because the code writes «label + number»; the radio says 一晩目, 二晩目… (3) Hatch: the count is the hide-and-seek いーち…じゅう！ and the final call もういいかい？; the death line is 「もういいかい？」……見つかった。 and the counting sheet in Hatch's den says もういいかい. The long-vowel mark ー gets a fixed vowel in the synthetic voice: harmless, it is a murmur. (4) The radio lines use kanji numerals because digits inside Japanese text are silent for the synthetic voice; every line was timed with the game's own syllable counter (src/engine/voice.ts) and fits before the next one (the fastest is night 1 «Gulpy…», at about 9 syllables per second). (5) Lampy: the radio «離してやれ。» deliberately echoes «ぜったいに離さないで» on her hospital bracelet, as «Lasciala andare» echoes «non lasciarla mai andare». (6) Fish names: the shortest natural puns, but katakana is longer than Chinese characters, so they go beyond the 2-5 of the brief: 50 have 4-5 characters, 42 have 6 and 8 have 7 (シラホネウナギ, ホネノオトシゴ, ヌリコメウツボ, ハカイシビラメ, コマ落ちテンス, 磁気切れウナギ, 見切れホウボウ, バイオレンザメ); 7 full-width characters are about as wide as 14 Latin letters, and they fit on one line in the catch card, the book title and the photo captions; glitch-family names use kanji technical words (二重, 巻き戻し, 砂嵐, 走査線, 圏外, 見切れ, 上書き). (7) Real species names: Japanese standard names (標準和名) where they exist, checked against Japanese sources (Japanese Wikipedia, zukan-bouz.com, the Toyosu imported-fish name list, WEB魚図鑑); less certain: ホンメルルーサ (Merluccius merluccius), オオハタ (Epinephelus marginatus), ヒラダイ (Sarpa salpa; its Japanese Wikipedia page is titled サルパ・サルパ), ヒカリホウボウ (a name proposed in 世界大博物図鑑), ツクシトビウオ (Cheilopogon heterurus, the Japanese subspecies), ニシイワシ (also called ヨーロッパマイワシ), チチュウカイフウライ. Species with no Japanese name use a katakana name printed by Japanese fish guides (スプラット, サルゴ, コモンスティングレイ, ペインテッドコンバー, ヨーロッパレインボーラス, トウェイトシャッド, アニュラーシーブリーム, グレーターウィーバー) or «〜の仲間» (a relative of a Japanese fish of the same genus or family), never an invented name. (8) The flyer: the draft texts read naturally and are kept as they are, so the Japanese font subsets (tools/render/fonts/annuncio/cjk/) need no rebuild; a native speaker might prefer the softer invito «日が沈むころ、古い桟橋で待ってるよ！» (日没 is slightly formal next to 待ってるよ), which would need new subsets (annuncio.py --sottoinsiemi). (9) The crayon drafts are kept: they are what a 6-9-year-old writes; IL MIO TESORO is Robin's, a boy, so ぼくのたからもの. 97ねん8がつ keeps the short year of AGOSTO 97 (a Japanese child of 1997 would more likely write へいせい9ねん, but the story is not set in Japan). (10) Marco Polo stays in Latin letters, as in the drawing (MARCO!/POLO!): Japanese players do not all know the pool game, but the death line 「Marco」……きみは答えた。 still reads as a call that should not have been answered.
